utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Unfortunately technology ruled the clock again this morning. I must apologise that it was not possible to commence at the appointed hour. I am told it is the product of a recent upgrade of the LiveNote system. There is an incompatibility which is yet to be tracked down. It's affecting all courts. When we broke last evening there was a question of some exhibits. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have those, Your Honour, and I would tender them now. I think there's no problem doing that in open session, as long as we don't talk about the content. All three of these I would move to be entered under seal. The first exhibit with the ERN number on the cover 03231371. Can I have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm just wanting to be sure we have the correct documents. The second one is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: U003-3397 on the cover. That's a document from 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is its date? The 29th of March, 1st of April. Yes. And the third?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The third is a single sheet of paper with some photographs, U003-8800.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which was an annex to an earlier statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. And I believe the Court's ruling yesterday is that this annex would be admitted but not the full statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the date of that statement to which it was annexed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would actually rather not say that in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. Those three exhibits will be received. With respect to the single photo sheet, are you tendering it or is it going to be the honour of Mr. Guy-Smith? Is there any distinction that we should be concerned about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't believe so, but I would be more than happy to take that honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I'm tendering it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good. Well, cooperation is what we like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was the one who entered that into the stream of testimony, that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first statement, ERN 03231371 will be Prosecution Exhibit P70, under seal. The second statement with ERN U003-3397 will be Prosecution Exhibit P71, under seal. And the photo line-up with ERN U003-8800 will be Prosecution Exhibit P72, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We are, I believe, ready for the next witness. Before that, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just raise one matter. I have spoken to the Prosecution about this matter. The witness who is about to give evidence has apparently, according to a document which we received yesterday, been interrogated by the Serb authorities. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, there has been investigation into these interviews, these interrogations. And the results of those investigations have been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So nothing more has been secured from the investigations than is presently known to the Defence; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Where are the notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not objecting. I just want to caution -- remind everybody that that witness was in closed session, so to avoid any specifics about the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been very careful not to indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think there's a problem at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So the position is that we do not have any notes of any interview. All we have is the fact that there were interviews and that's as far as it goes. So I would ask that this is expedited so that in -- well, I see somebody is shaking their head. If there are notes of the interviews, then where are they and why do we not have them?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I thought I answered the question the first time. To the extent we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you answered it without any detail. Have the investigations gone as far as it attempting to secure what information is known to the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have obtained the notes of interviews of certain interviews, not all interviews, conducted by the Serbian authorities. To the extent they relate to this case, are relevant to this case, those we have provided to the Defence. We have also, as the Defence is also well aware we have interviewed the person who was identified yesterday as having conducted that interview and questions were put to that individual about interviews he had conducted. And that was also provided to the Defence. That is as far -- in other words, to the extent we have records of interviews of witnesses in this case by Serb authorities, those have been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the point is that you have sought them in respect of all witnesses affected by this issue. You have secured them only in respect of some. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's not exactly correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have sought generally records from the Serb authorities pertaining to this case. And we have received records and we've gone through those records. And to the extent they relate to this case, we've provided them to the Defence. I cannot say that we have gone to the Serb authorities and said -- well, with respect to each possible witness, do you have interview notes of -- notes of interviews of that witness? That we have not done. However, we have, as I said, with the individual, the MUP inspector who was referenced yesterday, we have interviewed him and talked to him about his investigation generally. I hope I'm being clear. I'm trying to be as clear as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you. The specific answer seems to be, Mr. Mansfield, that general request for all available information has led to the provision of some information. And there has not been more specifically directed inquiry about matters that are not presently available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that and so far as it goes, it is of some use; we say not a lot. But in relation to the witness who is about to come, he plainly -- we have a date for that, but we have no idea what he actually said. And if the Prosecution from their inquiries know what he told the Serb authorities because there is a record, please may we have it before we cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand the answer to be that they have not got that. Is that correct, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that you are not in any way taking any further steps to attempt to secure that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At this time, we have not taken any further steps to secure that. I'm happy -- the fact is: Many records -- many of these records were destroyed in the war in Kosovo when certain buildings were bombed. But I'm happy, of course, to submit a request about -- that are specific to witnesses in this case to see if there are any further records that can be obtained. I'm happy to do that. I think it's also something that is -- that the Defence can do. They can make their own such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, well I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. May we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it might be prudent. It will remove some restraints. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, to -- yes, it's required, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is your ethnicity Kosovar Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the year 1998. At that time, did you have any problems with Serb authorities in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just -- it was a ranger, a forest ranger, and he was a Serb. Just with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what the problem was that you had with this forest ranger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this forest ranger, his name was Cedo, and he couldn't -- he wouldn't let me get firewood. And I problems with him for that reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this forest ranger try to get something from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a ranger for the forest in the mountain. And his name was Cedo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ask you for money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A hundred marks, Deutschmarks. And give him also a lamb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did -- why did he ask you for this money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he hated me. Well, I did not have a hundred marks, a hundred Deutschmarks, and I did -- for that reason, because he asked me for money, I went to other forests to get the wood, because I could not do -- I could not get the wood there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because he didn't give you the proper permit since you didn't give him the money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to avoid certain areas or certain roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did not go -- I did not dare to go on the asphalted road. I went on side roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness, can you tell us why you did not dare to go on the asphalted roads.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he could catch me and punish me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, still talking about the year 1998, the beginning part of the year, in the spring of 1998, were you, sir, a supporter of the LDK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you still a supporter of the LDK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I still support the LDK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again talking about 1998, the spring, did you start to hear anything about the KLA at that time? And again, I would caution you, if -- I would caution you not to identify the area where you lived. Just speak generally about what you heard, if anything, about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I have heard -- I did not hear anything about which areas there were soldiers in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else did you hear about the KLA? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that the KLA has been founded and that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about trenches being dug?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the -- did anybody from the KLA ask you to do anything, again in 1998, the spring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you were not yourself a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that we go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May the shutters go up?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I won't be showing anything on the screens for -- until the end, so for now there's no problem with the shutters going up. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would remind you again to make sure you do not use your name. The room that you were taken to that you described as a prison, can you describe that room for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were the yard gates there, entrance gate. There was a well there in front. There was soft manure under my feet where I was staying. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big was the room that you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 2 by 3. 2 metres by 3 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the floor made of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no floor. It was concrete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there was manure on the floor. Was there anything else on the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the manure where -- when I was beaten on that. Well, we weren't -- did not dare to go out and see anything. I know that there was manure where I was beaten and the prison where I stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll talk about when you were beaten in a moment. If we could just now talk about the room that you were kept in. What was on the floor of that room, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was nothing on the floor. In the room where we stayed, it was cement. It was cement. There was a hose there and there was water, and that is where I stayed. There was water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up there. Up. Somewhere -- it was leaking, the water was leaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the water leaking from? You said "up there." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no tap. It was from up there. I don't know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "up there," do you mean the ceiling of the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the ceiling. Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did the water that was leaking from the ceiling go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the ceiling it fell on us. And it stayed there until it dried up. It leaked a little. The floor got wet and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the room have a window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a very small window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it just one window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just one, only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the temperature in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The temperature, I don't know how to tell you, well as if somebody had set fire to the place. It was very hot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have enough air in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, what air?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what did you do when you needed to use the toilet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never went to a bathroom. There was a toilet inside there for two or three weeks. Then they brought a kind of a bucket, and that's where we had -- we relieved ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the first two or three weeks, where did you relieve yourselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the door in the corner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the floor there, behind the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When there was a bucket, was the bucket emptied regularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When it became full, sometimes it overflowed. When they felt like emptying it, they came and emptied it. When they didn't, it stayed like that, full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever take the bucket out of the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once. Only once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you take the bucket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a toilet a little further. That is where I emptied it and brought it back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were you given food when you were in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Food? Mostly we went without food than with food. Three or four days we stayed without food. Sometimes they gave us food, sometimes for 24 hours they didn't. Sometimes they brought us food -- they brought us food. But for three or four days we stayed -- we went without food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were given food, what were you given for food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pasta, a piece of bread; that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were you given water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was enough water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who brought the water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shala brought the water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did a doctor ever come to care for any of the people in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever allowed to leave the room and walk around the yard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Only Shala sometimes opened the door to air the room in the evening after sunset. So we could get out a little bit and then we went in again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that happen every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Once a week, once every three or four days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did guards ever come into the room for any reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in our room? Yes, yes. There came some soldiers -- yes, some guards came in. It was Shala and Murrizi, someone called Murrizi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did they come into the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came when they brought us food and they asked us sometimes, How do you feel? Are you okay?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you -- were you ever able to hear things happening to prisoners outside the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. We could hear shouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe those shouts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they shouted, people who were beaten. We could hear the voices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could hear the shouts of people who were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were persons ever beaten in the room you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were -- during the two months that -- or almost two months that you were there, were other prisoners brought into that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Yes, some. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did it happen that prisoners were taken out and not brought back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They brought them at night and they also took them out at night. So I couldn't -- I did not get to know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the -- can you recall the most number -- the largest number of prisoners that were ever in that room at one time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The largest number at -- in the evening -- in the latter part of my detention, there were many. So there were many people in the room, 12 or 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the prisoners speak with one another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't dare to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you dare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because Shala told us, If I see anyone speak to somebody else, there -- I will punish you. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you have referred a number of times to Shala. Can you tell us, please, what was Shala's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention Shala. I know Shala, because for two months, almost two months, he was there. He gave us bread and food. He served us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what else he did there. What was his job -- what was his function or job at the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. How could I know? He just gave us food and he had the keys to the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would he then let people in and out of the room you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He knew who came in and who got out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you see Shala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe him, please. What did he look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a moustache and he was a little bit swarthy. He had training shoes. He came there and brought us food and water. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he was a little bit swarthy, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had dark -- he was dark and his teeth were a little bit rotten. But he was tall and big and had a moustache.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he was talking about, are you able to tell us approximately how tall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, taller than me and bigger than me, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How tall are you? If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how tall I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say he was big, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, bigger than me. A little bigger than me and his face was skinny a little bit. He had a moustache, but the moustache was a little bigger at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he was bigger than you, do you mean he was -- was he fat? Was he overweight? Was he ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little fatter than me, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little fatter than you. How old do you think he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, probably 50 years old, 50, 52. Maybe he's not that old, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were first interviewed by UNMIK/CCIU and then by the ICTY, did you then provide a description of Shala during those interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I described him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you describe him the same way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the way he is. That's how I described him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you learned Shala's real name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shala, after the war I heard people and there were some occasions where I met people and I heard that he was Haradin Bala, but at that time we -- he was called "Shala," and I did not know his surname or name. Just Shala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was only after the war that you learned that Shala was Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you learned that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard people say, and more or less -- he has some acquaintances there and I heard what his name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the people who told you or talked about Shala being Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not me. I heard. It's things I heard from people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people in your village? People elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that you heard from that Shala was Haradin Bala.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard from my village there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear what village Haradin Bala was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard from Stankoc, close to Komorane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Haradin Bala after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see him in Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see him in Stimlje. Somebody else saw him. I haven't. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it that saw him in Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was seen by my brother, one of my brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the war, when is the first time that you saw Shala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the war, I never saw Shala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about on television, in connection with this case? Have you seen Shala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on television, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it that you saw on television that you thought was Shala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Shala. I recognised him very well. I was there for two months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was it that you saw on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shala, the way he was, he was on TV that way. And he was on TV. And I knew about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he on television in connection with this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. He was on TV. He appeared on TV. This commander, he was like this or like that. They were saying those things on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw him on television before this case started? Let me rephrase that. You saw him on television before the arrests in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, after the war. It was after the war that I saw him on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what you saw on television was nothing to do with this trial or this case, it was something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At this point I would object. It's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just trying to clarify the answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think the witness is doing a fine job himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, carry on, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't understand. Shala, as Shala, I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen on television any of this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you watched the television in this trial, did you recognise Shala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the person you knew as Shala in the courtroom here today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At this point in time, I would object to such an identification being made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, the witness can continue. We have already indicated the issue of [inaudible] is alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I think you started to answer the question but I'll put it to you again. Do you see the person you knew as Shala in the courtroom here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for us, please, where he is seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shala is in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the middle where in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the middle of Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he to your right or to your left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand. He is in the middle, in the middle between them two, Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu. Isak Musliu is on the right, Limaj is on the left. In the middle is Haradin Bala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which row? Is he in the front row? The second row?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Second row.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the record reflect that he's identified the accused Haradin Bala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when somebody came to the room to ask the prisoners in the room why they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We were there lying on the ground and couldn't dare raise our heads until next morning. Then they brought those three, four people I said. I don't know them. It was dark. We were not allowed to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, I'm not going to ask you anymore questions about that topic. I'm asking you about a different topic now. Was there a time when you were in that room when somebody else, a different person, came to the room to ask the people in the room why they were there, for what reason they were in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This Fatmir Limaj came and asked us. He said, You, you, why are you here for? And then he asked me and I said, I don't know. I went to look for my cousin. And they brought me here. I don't know why. He said, If you have something -- if you have done something, you will be killed. If you are innocent, you will go home. That's all. And I will come back in a week, he said. And when the week was over he came and said, You go home. The one who brought you here will suffer three times more than you because you have done nobody any harm. So you have to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a few questions about what you have just told us. You said that it was Fatmir Limaj who came to your room. Did you know at the time that it was Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. It was the first time for me to see him. Then I saw him on television later. And I want to thank him for releasing him [as interpreted], because maybe I would be still there or maybe I wouldn't be alive at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he came to the room, was he alone or was he with other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was alone. He was alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody let him into the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody. He came alone. From the door he asked us. Nobody entered the room with him. He was standing at the door and asked us why we were there and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Maybe I question was unclear. Did somebody unlock the door of the room for him? If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shala did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this person that you later learned was Fatmir Limaj, could you describe him, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the first time for me to see him. Then I remembered seeing him on television later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what did he look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was young. I don't know how to describe him. The same Fatmir Limaj that is here. Then after the war I saw him on television. I remember it was the same person. We didn't have any more contacts. It was just a two-, three-minute contact for me to see him and remember him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw him only those two times that you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only during those two times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about how he looked those two times, what he was wearing, how he looked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had -- was wearing KLA clothes without a hat. We didn't speak much, only a few words. You go home, or, Why are you here for? It lasted only one, two minutes the encounter, not more. I will look into your matter, he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second time he came, did he come alone or did he come with others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I saw him alone. He was standing at the door. We didn't -- couldn't see more than that. I wasn't interested. He came to the door and he told me, You can go home. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your two meetings or encounters with the person you later learned was Fatmir Limaj, were you able to tell what his role was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I know that they released me. I didn't know before what Fatmir Limaj was. I hadn't heard anything about him. I know that they let us go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break you told us that you learned after the war that the person you say released you from Lapusnik was Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please ask the witness to come closer to the mike, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn that this person from Lapusnik was Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the war when I saw him on television and when I heard people saying that this is Fatmir Limaj, this is how I came to know him. Because there, in the prison, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see him doing on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just saw him when he appeared on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it before he was arrested in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the war, after the war, not before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think my question was unclear. Did you see him on television before he was arrested in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, after the arrest. After he was arrested. After the war, I have seen him on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after the war did you see him on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After one year, because we didn't have a television set then. But then we managed to put up enough money to buy one and then I saw him on television. When he appeared, we saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year did the war end?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what year was it you saw him on television for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember the years. I know that it was after the war, after we were liberated. And then I don't know. I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was it one year after the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one year, yes. After one year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw him on the television, did he appear -- was he appearing in -- what you saw on the television, was it in Kosovo or was it here in The Hague? Was he, Fatmir Limaj, in Kosovo or here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in Kosova. In Kosova. I saw him in civilian clothes and I recognised his face. I recognised that it was him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise it right away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Once you saw him, I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reaction when you recognised him on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw him on television, I felt good because it was him who released me from prison and who saved my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any doubt, sir, that it was Fatmir Limaj who released you from prison in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the one who released me, and that's why I am home now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see Fatmir Limaj here in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe, please, where he is seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is on the left side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The left -- the left side of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On my left side. Can I see him? Look at him?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course you may look at him. Do you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see him. He is on the left side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your left side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On my left side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You previously identified Haradin Bala as Shala. Can you tell us where Fatmir Limaj is in relation to Haradin Bala.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right is Isak Musliu; in the middle is Haradin Bala; on the left is Limaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "on the right," and "on the left," is that your right and left or the left of Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I could suggest, you might try colour of ties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me put the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me adopt the suggestion of the Court. Could -- are you able to see what colour tie Fatmir Limaj is wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A grayish. Like dark, darkish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the record reflect that the witness has identified Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness by words and position appeared not to be, but by colour of tie appears certainly to be identifying Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just so the record is absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about Isak Musliu. What colour tie is he wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I look at it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Red.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would suggest now the record is -- the identification is clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The colour of ties, the record might note, appears to indicate that the accused [sic] was -- when speaking of right and left was speaking in the opposite sense to which the Chamber at least was understanding his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to -- I think the -- either the transcript or the Court misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, it's me again. I've done it before. I meant witness and not accused. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm moving on to another topic now, and that is the end of your time at Lapusnik. I believe before the break you said that there came a day when you were taken out of the room when the Serbs attacked Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took -- who took you out of the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Serb forces attacked Lapusnik. Haradin Bala and Murrizi came and told us, You will all come out and get your hand -- yourselves by the hand and run towards the mountain. And we held each other's hands and then we walked towards the fields. Shala was in -- was up front, Murrizi in the rear, and then we started to walk up the mountain and came up to a meadow. There was -- one of the prisoners had his leg wounded and they could walk slowly. After we arrived at this place, this meadow, there was a civilian who told Shala, Can I take you -- give you a lift? He said, Go away. And he didn't give us -- any of us a lift. And then we resumed walking again slowly up to Berisa Mountains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions about what you've just told us. How did you know that the Serb forces were attacking Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because they shelled it and they were -- we were in danger of being killed where we were. That's why they asked us to leave the place and to take the direction Berisa Mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day that happened, can you describe for us the condition you were in, the physical condition you were in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was -- I felt very weak, exhausted, unable to talk and to walk. More -- my -- the others pushed me and helped me because it was so hard for me to walk and to talk. And even after a month I went home, I couldn't open my mouth so exhausted I felt and tired out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about seeing a civilian along the way who spoke with Shala. What did he ask Shala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked Shala -- there was one of them a lame -- man was lame. And I said, Shall I give him a lift? Shala said, No. And then the other prisoners helped him to the -- up to the place where we arrived. It was a kind of meadow or field. On both sides there were mountains. This is the place where we stayed for two hours, for some two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just to be clear about this, who was it who asked if he should give a lift? Was it you or the civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that civilian -- that man in civilian clothes, I didn't know him. It was a civilian. He asked Shala, Can I give him a lift because he can hardly walk, he is wounded, to help him? Shala said, No. He said, You go your way. You mind your business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the man who could hardly walk was one of the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was someone else. He was not one of us prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he come with you from the -- from Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would object to this leading question at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We were going up the hill and he was descending. He was a civilian. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the man who was injured in the leg and could hardly walk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will note the objection. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this man come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the prison. Where we left the prison, there were about 20 or 30 people and he was there. I don't know where he came from. They Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pulled us all together and headed towards the Berisa Mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man who was injured in the leg you said came from the prison. Was -- had he been in the same room with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was not in the same room with me. He was elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your group there were men from your room as well as other rooms at Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the men who were not in your room, could you tell where they came from, what rooms they came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I saw them only when they asked us to leave the prison. I don't know where they came from. We just gathered some 20, 30 people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that day was the first time you had seen those other men who were not in your room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you saw that man with the car who offered the ride -- the lift, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing happened. Again, we started walking up to this meadow I said surrounded by mountains, Berisa Mountains. And we sat there for some two hours. After that, this Shala asked Murrizi to go to Berisa Mountains and to look for some bread for us because we hadn't eaten anything for four days and four nights. This Murrizi said, There is no bread. Because there were a lot of civilians around. We stayed there for some more time and then Shala told us, You, you, you, and you, stand apart. You are going home and the others will be released later because you are many. And then he moved us apart some 100 metres away from the others, nine or ten people we were I think. He gave us a piece of paper where it was written our name and last name and he said, Go home now. The others we left there. I don't know anything what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Murrizi went to get some bread but was unable to get any bread. Did you have any food at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. For four nights and four days we didn't eat anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on that last day while you were waiting for some two hours, did you -- were you able to have any food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to have any water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a well there and we could drink some water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want you to say the names, but -- or I don't want you to say any names, but when Shala told you -- said, You, you, you, and you, stand apart, you are going to be released, did he identify those people by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Only he pinpointed at them and said, You, you, you, and you, stand apart. And we parted from the others. We didn't know what was going to happen. And then Shala came and said, You will go home, but we will release the others later because you are too many to release all of you. Maybe someone can kill you on the way or do something wrong to you. There were I think ten of us and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go then, your group of ten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He accompanied us some 100 metres away from the others. He gave us a piece of paper where it was written the name and the last name and said, Go home now, but mind you, you should go to us our own checkpoints. Go to Kizhareke. They will tell you where to go. We took those slips of paper and went to Kizhareke. There were some soldiers there, and some civilians and they put us into a shop. We rested there a while. We showed them the pieces of paper, waiting there for half an hour. They brought a tractor there, put us on the tractor, on top of the tractor, and they took us to Kroimire. In Kroimire the soldiers talked to the commander and told him to release us at 8.00. Let them go where they want, and if something happens, you are responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commander in Kroimire, do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you released from Kroimire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A soldier came that night. His name was Luani. I don't know who he was. It was night, it was dark. Guarded us until 8.00 in the morning. When 8.00 came, we went to the commander and he told us, Go where you want now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 29th day of November, 2004, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
